title: Edwards Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Edwards wells have a median depth of 185 feet, with fractured mountain bedrock affecting yield and drilling cost.
h1: Edwards, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land around Edwards means looking past the listing and into the well record. Within five miles, Colorado DWR records show 876 permitted wells, although only 357 are recorded as constructed. Of those, 473 report total depth, 222 report pump yield, and 57 report static water level.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, and most name an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer. That makes nearby well records useful for planning, but not a guarantee for a particular lot. Ground conditions, access, casing, grout, pump design, and the exact bedrock fracture system all affect the result.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Edwards?
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Edwards is 185 feet. The middle half runs from 80 to 307 feet, which is the range a buyer should keep in mind when comparing drilling bids. A driller may encounter water much shallower or need to continue substantially deeper on the same mountain slope.

The depth mix shows that 29% of wells are under 100 feet, 40% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 27% are between 300 and 600 feet. Four percent are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest record reaches 1,500 feet. For a proposed lot, nearby wells on similar geology and elevation are more useful than the countywide median alone.

sections.heading: Expected well yield in Edwards
sections.html:
Reported yields are generally strong: the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 15.0 to 20.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-five percent of reporting wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 22% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 3% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. No reporting wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures describe tested well capacity, not a promise of continuous household flow. In fractured granite and gneiss, a productive fracture can be close to a dry hole. Ask for the well completion report, pump test information, storage capacity, and any history of pressure or seasonal problems before relying on the headline yield.

sections.heading: Water levels and the local record
sections.html:
The median static water level is 65 feet below ground surface, with the middle half from 25 to 190 feet. That spread matters when estimating pump setting, trench depth, and the electrical system. A shallow static level does not necessarily mean a shallow drilling target; the well still has to reach a water-bearing fracture.

The decade series does not show a simple falling water table in these records. Median depth to water was 114 feet in the 1990s, 25 feet in the 2010s, and 32 feet in the 2020s. The measurements are limited to 57 wells and may reflect different locations, seasons, and measurement conditions. Treat them as local clues rather than a basinwide trend.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Edwards, and when?
sections.html:
Permit activity is concentrated in the late twentieth century. The records show 305 permits issued in the 1990s, 131 in the 1980s, 125 in the 2000s, 89 in the 2010s, and 32 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. Older permits can still help identify local depth and geology, but their equipment, construction standards, and use may differ from a new well.

Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, including Shelton and Joe Wayne, appears most often with 281 records. Shelton Drilling Corporation, including Shelton and Wayne, appears on 45, and Authorized, including Pe and Pg, appears on 36. Compare records from Edwards with nearby Avon, Wolcott, and Eagle rather than assuming one driller's historical results fit every parcel.

sections.heading: What a new well costs near Edwards
sections.html:
Edwards drilling is in fractured mountain bedrock described as granite and gneiss. The drilling rate in the cost model is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 185-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $12,000 to $18,500.

A finished well is a larger project. Adding the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical brings the modeled total to about $18,000 to $30,500 at the median depth. A bid can move outside that range when the hole must go deeper, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the site needs substantial trenching. Get the drilling, completion, pump, and site-work allowances in writing instead of comparing only the per-foot rate.

sections.heading: Edwards risks to check before building
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main pattern in the reported data, but fractured-bedrock wells remain unpredictable. A neighboring high-yield well does not rule out a dry hole on your parcel. Confirm the permit status, permitted use, well construction, test yield, static level, and any pump or storage limitations. Domestic use, stock, irrigation, and monitoring permits do not all provide the same practical water supply.

Water quality also deserves separate attention. Within about ten miles, the mapping shows 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 36 historic mine features, and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not establish contamination at a house, but it supports testing existing water and reviewing the property history. Septic separation, driveway access, drilling equipment access, building location, and electrical routing should be evaluated before finalizing a homesite.

sections.heading: Buying or building on an Edwards lot
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's Colorado DWR permit record and then compare several nearby wells with similar slope, elevation, and bedrock. The 185-foot median and 80-to-307-foot middle half are useful for budgeting, while the 65-foot median static level helps frame pump and trench planning. They are not substitutes for a site-specific drilling proposal.

Have the seller provide the well construction report, pump test, water-quality results, and permit documents. If the lot has no well, confirm that a new permit can support the intended household use and coordinate the well location with the septic system, building envelope, access route, and utility trench. In over-appropriated basins, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses. A Colorado water attorney or qualified well contractor can review that question before closing.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Edwards, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Edwards is 185 feet. The middle half ranges from 80 to 307 feet. Twenty-nine percent are under 100 feet, while 27% are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,500 feet, so local geology and the exact lot still control the final depth.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Edwards?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 185-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $12,000 to $18,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $18,000 to $30,500. Difficult access or greater depth can raise the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Edwards?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 15.0 to 20.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-five percent of reporting wells exceed 15 gallons per minute. Results are not guaranteed because mountain bedrock depends on fractures, and a strong neighboring well does not ensure the same result on another lot.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Edwards?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from yield or depth. The area within about ten miles has 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 36 historic mine features, and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing or new well for locally relevant contaminants and general drinking-water indicators, and review the property's history before relying on the water.

faq.q: Can I build a home on a lot with a well near Edwards?
faq.a: You need to verify the well permit, permitted use, construction record, water supply, and septic layout before building. Most nearby records are domestic or household wells, but uses differ. Coordinate the well, septic system, building site, driveway, and utilities early. In an over-appropriated basin, some proposed uses may also require an augmentation plan.
